# Executive summary

This paper specifies the finite latent-progress extension to JoiNMe. JoiNMe
models multivariate longitudinal outcomes through nested mixed effects and can
jointly model a time-to-event process through current-value, current-slope,
correlation and covariance associations. The extension introduces
heterogeneity by replacing the centred distribution of selected standardised
random effects with a finite location--scale mixture.

The implementation has six defining properties.

1. The public entry point is `joinme_mix()`, with fitted and predicted
   subclasses that inherit the existing JoiNMe interface.
2. Two latent-progress coordinates are selected per block by default.
3. Classes are attached to random-effect allocation units: subjects for
   subject and covariance-regression effects, markers for marker effects and
   marker weights.
4. Combining levels retains \(G\) classes. Compatible blocks share one
   allocation rather than producing a Cartesian product.
5. Discrete allocations are marginalised exactly in Stan.
6. A longitudinal-only form, available from both `joinme()` and
   `joinme_mix()`, removes the survival likelihood exactly whilst retaining
   the common model-building infrastructure.

The same model now has a direct generative implementation through
`simulate_joinme_mix()`. This simulator samples the otherwise marginalised
class allocations, generates selected standardised latent coordinates from
their component distributions, and delegates all remaining longitudinal and
event generation to `simulate_joinme()`. Simulation and fitting therefore
share their formula parsing, coordinate selection, allocation domains and
component-family convention.

The result is a bespoke but restrained extension. It changes the random-effect
distribution without duplicating the longitudinal likelihood, survival
likelihood, transformations, prediction programme or diagnostics.

# Scientific motivation

Multivariate longitudinal data often show more heterogeneity than a single
elliptical random-effect distribution can express. Two subjects may have
similar observed values at baseline but differ systematically in their
long-term direction. Conversely, two subjects may have similar mean
trajectories but markedly different covariance or volatility patterns.
Markers can also form classes according to their population deviations or
their importance in a survival association.

A finite latent-progress distribution offers a probabilistic description of
such heterogeneity. It is preferable to classifying estimated random effects
after model fitting for three reasons.

- Longitudinal measurement error and shrinkage are propagated into class
  uncertainty.
- Survival information can contribute to estimation when a joint model is
  fitted.
- Class locations, scales, proportions and random effects are estimated
  jointly rather than in a sequential plug-in procedure.

The word *latent* is important. A class is an unobserved component of a
statistical distribution, not an observed diagnosis. Posterior allocation
probabilities, sensitivity analysis and predictive assessment are therefore
central to interpretation.

# Generative latent-progress simulation

## Simulation-to-fit correspondence

Let \(C_j\) be the class of allocation unit \(j\). The simulator first draws

\[
C_j\sim\operatorname{Categorical}(\boldsymbol{\pi}_j)
\]

and then, for every selected packed coordinate \(r\),

\[
Z_{jr}\mid C_j=g
\sim
D(\mu_{gr},s_{gr}).
\]

The fitted Stan programme evaluates the marginal density

\[
p(\boldsymbol Z_j)
=
\sum_{g=1}^{G}
\pi_{jg}
\prod_{r=1}^{K}
p_D(Z_{jr}\mid\mu_{gr},s_{gr})
\]

with `log_sum_exp`. Thus the discrete simulation and marginalised fitting
programme describe the same probability model.

The ordinary covariance transformations are applied only after component
sampling:

\[
\boldsymbol u_i=L_u\boldsymbol z_{u,i},
\qquad
\boldsymbol v_d=L_v\boldsymbol z_{v,d},
\qquad
L_i=L_i(\boldsymbol z_{L,i}).
\]

This ordering prevents component locations from changing meaning when the
ordinary random-effect scales change.

## Generative parameters

The fitting syntax is retained through `n_classes`, `formulaClass`,
`class_type`, `class_dimensions`, and `class_ordering`.
`class_parameters` supplies values that must be fixed in a data-generating
mechanism:

- baseline class probabilities;
- class-regression coefficients;
- component locations; and
- positive component scales.

The class probabilities are normalised to a simplex. Formula intercepts are
excluded because the simplex already defines the zero-covariate probabilities.
Named coefficients are aligned with the class-design columns saved in the
truth record.

## Shared allocations

Subject and covariance-regression coordinates share a subject allocation.
Marker effects use a marker allocation. This is the generative counterpart of
the fitted model's single `log_sum_exp` per natural allocation unit.

## Simulation truth and blinding

The complete generative record is returned under `truth$mixture`, including
unit-specific probabilities, realised allocations, component parameters and
standardised draws. True labels are deliberately absent from `dataLong` and
`dataEvent`. Recovery studies must join them only after fitting; otherwise a
class label can inadvertently become an observed predictor.

## Recovery-study estimands

A rigorous study should report component-location and scale bias, interval
coverage, baseline and covariate-dependent class-probability recovery,
posterior probability assigned to the true class, entropy, multiclass proper
scores, outcome prediction, survival discrimination and convergence.
Simulation factors should include component overlap, rare classes, sample
size, marker count, response families, shrinkage family, censoring,
association strength and fitted class-count misspecification.

# Base JoiNMe model

For subject \(i\), marker \(d\), and time \(t\), the longitudinal predictor
is

\[
\eta_{id}(t)
=
\boldsymbol x_{id}(t)^\top\boldsymbol\beta
+
\boldsymbol z_i(t)^\top\boldsymbol u_i
+
\boldsymbol z_d(t)^\top\boldsymbol v_d
+
\boldsymbol z_{id}(t)^\top\boldsymbol w_{id}.
\]

The response follows marker-specific family \(\mathcal F_d\) with inverse link
\(g_d^{-1}\). Ancillary parameters can have their own distributional
regressions.

The realised subject and marker effects are

\[
\boldsymbol u_i=L_u\boldsymbol z_{u,i},\qquad
\boldsymbol v_d=L_v\boldsymbol z_{v,d}.
\]

The nested subject-by-marker effect is

\[
\boldsymbol w_{id}
=
\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol r_w)L_i\boldsymbol z_{w,id}.
\]

The subject covariance factor \(L_i\) is generated through lower-triangular
regression predictors. For entry \(m\),

\[
\ell_{im}
=
\alpha_{L,m}
+
\boldsymbol x_{\mathrm{cov},i}^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta_{L,m}
+
\lambda_{L,m}z_{L,im}.
\]

The event hazard for cause \(k\) is

\[
h_{ik}(t)
=
h_{0k}(t)
\exp\left[
\boldsymbol x_{S,i}(t)^\top\boldsymbol\gamma_k
+
A_i(t)
\right],
\]

where \(A_i(t)\) is a sum of active transformed association channels.

# Latent-progress model

## Component distribution

Let \(\mathcal K\) denote the selected standardised coordinates after the
requested blocks have been concatenated. For class \(g\),

\[
a_{rk}\mid C_r=g,\mu_{gk},s_{gk}
\sim D_\nu(\mu_{gk},s_{gk}),
\qquad k\in\mathcal K.
\]

The component family is selected through the existing `shrinkage` convention:

| `shrinkage` | component \(D_\nu\) |
|---:|---|
| 0 | Student-\(t\), 6 degrees of freedom |
| 1 | Laplace |
| 2 | Normal |

The finite mixture is

\[
p(\boldsymbol a_r)
=
\sum_{g=1}^{G}
\pi_g
\prod_{k\in\mathcal K}
D_\nu(a_{rk};\mu_{gk},s_{gk}).
\]

The component covariance is diagonal on the selected standardised scale. The
existing Cholesky factors remain responsible for correlations in realised
subject and marker random effects.

## Class proportions and component priors

\[
\boldsymbol\pi\sim
\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\boldsymbol\alpha_\pi),
\]

\[
s_{gk}\sim\operatorname{Exponential}(1).
\]

By default, Stan orders only the first selected random-intercept location
across classes. Slope and other location coordinates remain unrestricted.
`class_ordering = "probability"` instead orders the baseline class
probabilities, and `"none"` imposes no order. There are no anchor values or
public anchor-scale controls.

`formulaClass` optionally regresses membership on allocation-unit covariates.
The simplex supplies the intercept. One formula uses class \(G\) as the
reference category; a list of \(G\) formulae supplies separate, compact
class-specific predictors and defaults to no ordering.
`jm_prior(class_probability = ...)` supplies
\(\boldsymbol\alpha_\pi\), whilst `class_regression` supplies the Normal prior
scale for the regression coefficients.

## Two-dimensional default

For an available block dimension \(q\), the default selected coordinates are

\[
\{1,\ldots,\min(2,q)\}.
\]

The one-dimensional special case is legitimate and is reported as such.
`class_dimensions` permits an explicit alternative.

# Four class types

## Subject effects

`class_type = "subject"` replaces the distribution of selected
\(\boldsymbol z_{u,i}\) coordinates. This is the most direct latent progression
model when the first two coordinates are a subject intercept and slope.

## Marker effects

`class_type = "marker"` replaces the distribution of selected
\(\boldsymbol z_{v,d}\) coordinates. The allocation unit is a marker. Survival
associations are not reparameterised; the class-specific marker trajectory can
nevertheless enter a current-value or current-slope association.

## Correlation effects

`class_type = "corr"` replaces selected off-diagonal correlation coordinates
of \(\boldsymbol z_{L,i}\). The coordinate indices refer to correlations only;
Stan maps them to their positions in the packed lower triangle.

## Variance--covariance effects

`class_type = "vcov"` replaces selected lower-triangular coordinates of
\(\boldsymbol z_{L,i}\), including scale coordinates. It classes subject
covariance profiles and does not assign a component distribution to every
\(\boldsymbol z_{w,id}\) innovation. `corr` and `vcov` cannot be selected
together because they describe the same latent block.

# Shared allocations and the meaning of \(G\)

The subject allocation domain contains `"subject"`, `"corr"`, and `"vcov"`.
The marker allocation domain contains `"marker"`.

For a combined subject-domain request:

\[
p(\boldsymbol z_{u,i},\boldsymbol z_{L,i})
=
\sum_{g=1}^G
\pi_g
p_g(\boldsymbol z_{u,i})
p_g(\boldsymbol z_{L,i}).
\]

The same \(g\) is used in both factors. Thus \(G=3\) gives three joint
subject-progress classes, not nine combinations.

If an subject block and a marker block are selected together, both use the
same \(G\) labels and \(\boldsymbol\pi\), but their posterior allocations are
reported over their natural units. This avoids the incoherent notion that an
subject and a marker share one observed allocation unit.

# Marginalisation in Stan

Hamiltonian Monte Carlo requires a differentiable continuous parameter space.
For allocation unit \(r\), Stan adds

\[
\log\sum_{g=1}^G
\exp\left\{
\log\pi_g+\log p_g(\boldsymbol a_r)
\right\}.
\]

Generated quantities calculate

\[
p_{rg}
=
\frac{\pi_gp_g(\boldsymbol a_r)}
{\sum_{h=1}^G\pi_hp_h(\boldsymbol a_r)}.
\]

These are conditional class probabilities for each posterior draw. The
reported probability is the posterior mean of \(p_{rg}\), with a credible
interval. A maximum-probability class is retained only for convenient tables
and plots.

# Exact replacement of the ordinary prior

The Stan model first applies the established ordinary prior. The mixture block
then adds

\[
\log p_{\mathrm{mix}}(\boldsymbol a_r)
-
\log p_{\mathrm{ordinary}}(\boldsymbol a_r).
\]

For subject, marker and covariance-regression standardised effects, the
ordinary denominator is Normal. For marker-weight perturbations it follows the
existing shrinkage family. This is an exact prior replacement.

If formula-scoped random-effect weights are present, the relevant log-density
terms are weighted consistently in the numerator and denominator.

# Survival associations under latent classes

The base association decomposition is unchanged.

- Mean channels use fixed plus subject effects.
- Marker channels use marker plus subject-by-marker effects.
- Total channels add mean and marker parts.
- Correlation and covariance channels use summaries of \(L_i\).

Weighted marker aggregation follows:

\[
\bar f_{a,i}(t)
=
\frac{1}{D}
\sum_{d=1}^D
\omega_{ad}^{\mathrm{eff}}
f_a\{r_{aid}(t)\}.
\]

Transformation occurs before marker averaging. If marker weights are
class-specific, the class component location supplies the weight perturbation for a
class-specific association curve.

The association coefficient remains common unless the underlying ordinary
model specifies otherwise. The mixture acts through its random-effect or
weight distribution; it does not introduce an undocumented class-specific
association coefficient.

# Longitudinal estimands

## Class centre

`mean_per_class` evaluates the inverse link after inserting component locations
for the selected random-effect blocks which enter the longitudinal location.
It answers:

> What trajectory is implied by the centre of this latent component at the
> chosen covariate profile?

## Marginal within class

`marginal_per_class` draws from the fitted within-component distribution and
then applies the inverse link. It answers:

> What response-scale trajectory is expected after acknowledging
> within-component random-effect variation?

These estimands are not interchangeable under a non-linear inverse link.

## Covariance class

If covariance regression receives a latent-class distribution, the dedicated display reconstructs the
covariance matrix for every class and posterior draw over the covariance
covariate grid. Every \(G\) curve appears in the same component panel, with a
separate returned plot for each marker.

The covariance-regression loading is coordinate-specific. If \(m\) indexes one
packed lower-triangular coordinate, \(\lambda_m\) is a non-negative scalar and
the full collection \(\boldsymbol\lambda\) is a vector of length
\(M_{\mathrm{cov}}\). In vector notation its action is
\(\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol\lambda)\boldsymbol z_{L,i}\), rather than a
dense loading matrix. In the ordinary model, \(\lambda_m\) is the residual
standard deviation of the untransformed covariance predictor. Under class
\(g\), the latent contribution has location
\(\lambda_m\mu_{gm}\) and distributional scale \(\lambda_ms_{gm}\); the
positive diagonal link or off-diagonal partial-correlation mapping is applied
afterwards.

# Longitudinal-only likelihood

When both event arguments are `NULL`, the implementation creates a private
event scaffold for common design construction, then sends zero event indicators
and zero integration limits to Stan. The event contribution is exactly

\[
0-\int_0^0h_i(s)\,ds=0.
\]

No survival information enters inference. Association terms and marker-weight
classes are disallowed. Event prediction and discrimination methods explain
that no event process was fitted, while longitudinal prediction and diagnostics
remain inherited.

# Software interface

The fitted hierarchy is:

```text
JoiNMeFit
└── JoiNMeMixFit

JoiNMeDynPred
└── JoiNMeMixDynPred
```

The following established methods remain available:

- `summary()`, `print()`, `plot()`;
- `predict()` and dynamic-prediction summaries;
- `draws()`, `extract()`, `fixef()`, `ranef()`, and `vcov()`;
- `posterior_linpred()`, `posterior_epred()`, and `posterior_predict()`;
- `pp_check()`, `diagnosis()`, and `mcmc_plot()`;
- `loo()`, `waic()`, and `elpd()`;
- `concordance()`, `tvROC()`, and `tvAUC()` for joint fits;
- `assoc()` and `posterior_assoc()`.

Mixture-specific additions are:

- `posterior_class()` for fitted units and dynamically predicted subjects;
- direct plotting of a `posterior_class()` result using posterior mean
  probabilities and central intervals;
- `type = "class_membership"`;
- `estimand = "mean_per_class"`;
- `estimand = "marginal_per_class"`;
- `type = "covariance_class"`;
- class-specific association trajectories.

`posterior_assoc()` distinguishes a coefficient from its realised class
contribution. The coefficient and marker weights remain common unless the
model explicitly states otherwise. When a selected class block changes the
longitudinal or covariance feature entering an association, the method appends
a compact class-by-reference-value table using `Estimate`, `Est.Error`,
`Q2.5`, `Q97.5`, `Rhat`, `ess_bulk` and `ess_tail`. Irrelevant class blocks do
not cause duplicated class rows.

The mixture summary distinguishes five inferential objects. Baseline class
probabilities are evaluated at zero-valued centred class covariates. Component
locations and within-class scales describe the selected standardised latent
random-effect coordinates and are reported in separate tables. The
class-membership regression reports estimated multinomial-logit contrasts;
for a shared class formula, the final class is the zero-coefficient reference.
The allocation table then reports the posterior distribution of the
draw-specific expected class count and the maximum-probability hard count,
without reproducing every unit-by-class row, which remains available through
`posterior_class()`. Posterior means, medians, standard deviations and central
interval endpoints are stored in distinct numeric columns because component
scales and probabilities need not have symmetric posterior distributions.

# Recommended analysis protocol

For mixture fits, the sampler audit includes a chain-level energy table and a
model-specific geometry audit. The latter reports posterior compensation
between the within-class component scale and the ordinary random-effect scale
through which that component is subsequently transformed. Strong negative
correlation indicates that the likelihood identifies their combination more
readily than the separate factors. The ranked correlation of posterior block
summaries with Hamiltonian energy is descriptive evidence about the difficult
direction, not a causal test of a parameter or a substitute for R-hat,
effective sample size, divergences and posterior predictive assessment.

## Model preparation

1. Establish marker families and links.
2. Establish the nested random-effect formula.
3. Check covariance regression without a mixture.
4. Check event-time representation and association transforms.
5. Fit the ordinary JoiNMe model and inspect posterior predictive adequacy.

## Mixture preparation

1. Name the allocation unit required by the scientific question.
2. Identify the two coordinates and record their formula labels.
3. Choose a small plausible range of \(G\).
4. Set weakly informative but meaningful component priors.
5. Decide whether Student-\(t_6\), Laplace or Normal components are defensible.

## Posterior review

1. Examine all sampler diagnostics.
2. Plot mixture proportions, locations and scales by chain.
3. Inspect posterior class probabilities.
4. Compare class-centre and marginal curves.
5. Inspect covariance or association curves when they define the class.
6. Check posterior predictions by marker.
7. Repeat under neighbouring values of \(G\) and prior settings.

# Choosing the number of classes

There is no single numerical criterion that establishes a scientifically valid
class count. A considered choice should combine:

- predictive measures;
- posterior predictive adequacy;
- stable estimation across chains;
- effective class size;
- posterior allocation entropy;
- separation of class-relevant estimands;
- sensitivity to priors and component family; and
- subject-matter interpretability.

A component containing a few observations may indicate a genuine rare
trajectory, a heavy tail, an outlier mechanism, or overfitting. These
possibilities should be distinguished through sensitivity analyses rather than
resolved by a modal label alone.

# Reporting template

## Methods

Report the nested longitudinal formula, marker families, event model,
association channels, covariance regression, class-specific levels, selected
coordinate labels, \(G\), component family and priors. State whether survival
was included and whether marker weights were shared.

## Results

Report class proportions with intervals, component locations and scales,
allocation uncertainty, centre and marginal trajectories, and any
class-defining covariance or association curves.

## Diagnostics

Report \(\widehat R\), effective sample sizes, divergent transitions,
tree-depth behaviour, posterior predictive checks, and sensitivity analyses.

## Interpretation

Describe classes as posterior components of a fitted model. Avoid implying
that they are error-free observed categories. Where decisions depend on class,
propagate posterior probabilities.

# Limitations

The implementation uses diagonal component scales on the selected standardised
coordinates. Correlation is retained through the underlying random-effect
Cholesky factors, but the component distribution does not add a second freely
estimated correlation matrix.

Intercept or baseline-probability ordering removes the corresponding label
permutation but does not guarantee scientifically meaningful separation. With
`class_ordering = "none"`, permutation-invariant summaries and careful
posterior inspection are particularly important.

Class-specific marginal longitudinal curves integrate the selected component
distribution. Covariance classes may primarily manifest through dispersion
rather than a shifted conditional mean.

Dynamic predictions inherit the fitted joint model and retain mixture
metadata. More importantly, dynamically sampled coordinates use the fitted
draw-specific component probabilities, locations and scales. The new
subject's history therefore updates a probability vector over classes;
the software does not treat their class as known. Combined compatible blocks
continue to contribute to one allocation density rather than independent
labels.

# Implementation audit trail

The R implementation is centred in:

```text
R/mix.R
R/mix-methods.R
R/standata.R
R/r6.R
R/plot-api.R
R/predict.R
```

The Stan implementation is centred in:

```text
inst/stan/joinme_mix_fit_threading.stan
inst/stan/joinme_mix_dynpred_threading.stan
inst/stan/helper/data/fit_mixture_data.stan
inst/stan/helper/data/dynpred_mixture_data.stan
inst/stan/helper/parameters/joinme_fit_mixture.stan
inst/stan/helper/functions/latent_progress_mixture.stanfunctions
inst/stan/helper/model/fit_mixture_priors.stan
inst/stan/helper/model/dynpred_mixture_prior.stan
inst/stan/helper/generated_quantities/fit_mixture_outputs.stan
inst/stan/helper/generated_quantities/dynpred_mixture_output_declarations.stan
inst/stan/helper/generated_quantities/dynpred_mixture_output_calculations.stan
```

The ordinary entry points and common likelihood modules are:

```text
inst/stan/helper/data/fit_data.stan
inst/stan/helper/parameters/joinme_fit_common.stan
inst/stan/joinme_fit_threading.stan
inst/stan/joinme_dynpred_threading.stan
inst/stan/helper/model/fit_threaded_likelihood.stan
inst/stan/helper/model/dynpred_threaded_likelihood.stan
```

The ordinary programmes do not include any mixture declaration or density.
R selects one of the four entry points before compilation and filters the
sampling data against that programme's own data contract. Thus latent-class
support does not enlarge the generated ordinary Stan model.

Transformation bytecode is a distinct, model-independent module:

```text
R/bytecode-interpreter.R
inst/stan/helper/bytecode/interpreter.stanfunctions
inst/stan/helper/bytecode/README.md
```

The R expression compiler consumes the module's opcode registry, and simulation
uses the same evaluator as preprocessing and plotting. The Stan implementation
mirrors the documented instruction protocol. Neither interpreter knows about
longitudinal outcomes, event processes or latent classes, which makes this
module suitable for later extraction into a separate package.

Focused regression tests are in:

```text
tests/testthat/test-latent-progress-mixture.R
```

The live architecture map is `notes/docs/architecture.md`; the statistical and
usage vignettes are under `vignettes/joinme-latent-progress-*.qmd`.
